concepts.name: Types of Emergencies: Classification and Constitutional Basis
key_dimensions: Three distinct types: National Emergency (Art. 352), President's Rule (Art. 356), Financial Emergency (Art. 360) — their separate constitutional homes
Common trap: Art. 352 is titled 'Proclamation of Emergency' but colloquially called 'National Emergency' — UPSC exploits this labeling
Comparison of triggering grounds across all three types and which type has never been proclaimed (Financial Emergency)
Distinction between 'Emergency' as a legal term vs. colloquial use, and why Art. 356 is not technically called 'Emergency' in the Constitution

concepts.name: Grounds for Proclamation of National Emergency (Art. 352)
key_dimensions: Original grounds: external aggression or war; 44th Amendment added 'armed rebellion' replacing 'internal disturbance' — a critical substitution UPSC tests
Written advice of Cabinet (not just PM) mandatory before President acts — 44th Amendment safeguard
Proclamation can be issued even before actual occurrence of war/aggression/armed rebellion if President is satisfied threat is imminent
Trap: 'Armed rebellion' vs. 'internal disturbance' — why the change matters constitutionally and politically (Indira Gandhi era misuse)

concepts.name: Parliamentary Approval and Continuation of National Emergency
key_dimensions: Must be approved by both Houses within one month by special majority (2/3 of members present and voting + majority of total membership)
Trap: If Lok Sabha is dissolved before approval, Rajya Sabha can approve, but Lok Sabha must ratify within 30 days of reconstitution
Continuation requires fresh approval every six months by special majority — unlike ordinary laws
44th Amendment requirement: special majority for approval, contrasted with simple majority under original Constitution

concepts.name: Revocation of National Emergency: Lok Sabha's Exclusive Power
key_dimensions: President must revoke if Lok Sabha passes a resolution by simple majority — Rajya Sabha has NO role here (UPSC trap: asymmetry between approval and revocation)
Special sitting of Lok Sabha: 1/10th of total membership can requisition a special sitting to pass revocation resolution
Revocation is by President's proclamation — he has no discretion once Lok Sabha passes the resolution
Contrast: Approval requires both Houses + special majority; Revocation requires only Lok Sabha + simple majority

concepts.name: Effects of National Emergency on Fundamental Rights
key_dimensions: Art. 358: Art. 19 suspended automatically during war/external aggression — NOT during armed rebellion (44th Amendment distinction — classic UPSC trap)
Art. 359: President can suspend right to move courts for enforcement of specified FRs (except Arts. 20 and 21 — 44th Amendment made these non-suspendable)
Art. 358 operates automatically; Art. 359 requires a separate Presidential Order — procedural difference
Art. 19 suspension under Art. 358 applies only against State action, not private parties; Art. 359 suspension is broader

concepts.name: Effects of National Emergency on Centre-State Relations
key_dimensions: Parliament acquires power to legislate on State List subjects (Art. 250) — but state legislatures are NOT suspended, they can still legislate
Executive power of Centre extends to giving directions to states on any matter (Art. 353)
Art. 354: President can modify provisions relating to distribution of revenues between Centre and states
Trap: Parliament's laws on State List during emergency continue for 6 months after emergency ends — not immediate cessation

concepts.name: Extension of Lok Sabha's Term During National Emergency
key_dimensions: Art. 83(2): Parliament can extend Lok Sabha's term by one year at a time during National Emergency — not indefinitely in one go
Extension can continue as long as emergency is in force, but each extension is only one year
Must cease within 6 months after emergency ends — Lok Sabha cannot continue beyond this
Trap: Rajya Sabha's term cannot be extended — it is a permanent body; only Lok Sabha's term is extendable

concepts.name: President's Rule (Art. 356): Grounds and Constitutional Mandate
key_dimensions: Two grounds: (a) Report of Governor OR (b) President's own satisfaction that state governance cannot be carried on per Constitution
Trap: President can act even without Governor's report ('otherwise') — this was misused historically
S.R. Bommai case (1994): Judicial review of President's satisfaction is permissible; floor test mandatory before dismissal of government
Art. 365: If state fails to comply with Union directions, it is ground for Art. 356 — often overlooked connection

concepts.name: Parliamentary Approval and Duration of President's Rule
key_dimensions: Must be approved by both Houses within 2 months by simple majority (contrast with National Emergency's special majority — major UPSC trap)
Initially for 6 months; can be extended up to 3 years with parliamentary approval every 6 months
Beyond 1 year: two additional conditions must be met — National Emergency must be in operation in whole/part of state, OR Election Commission certifies elections cannot be held
Trap: Rajya Sabha can approve even if Lok Sabha is dissolved — both Houses needed (unlike National Emergency revocation)

concepts.name: Effects of President's Rule on State Legislature and Executive
key_dimensions: President assumes functions of state government; Governor acts as President's agent
State legislature: can be dissolved OR kept under suspended animation (prorogued) — President has discretion on which
When legislature is dissolved: Parliament legislates for the state; when suspended animation: President's ordinances
Trap: Laws made by Parliament for a state during President's Rule continue even after its revocation — they don't automatically lapse

concepts.name: S.R. Bommai Case (1994): Judicial Review of President's Rule
key_dimensions: Supreme Court held: President's satisfaction under Art. 356 is subject to judicial review on grounds of mala fide or irrelevant/extraneous grounds
Floor test is the best test of majority — President cannot dismiss government without giving it a chance to prove majority
If proclamation is held unconstitutional, court can restore dissolved legislature and dismissed government
Secularism as basic feature: anti-secular activities by state government can be ground for Art. 356 — controversial but settled law

concepts.name: Revocation and Scope of President's Rule
key_dimensions: President can revoke at any time — no parliamentary approval needed for revocation (contrast with National Emergency)
President can transfer state functions to himself but cannot transfer state legislative power to Parliament without Parliament's authorization
Trap: President cannot authorize High Court's powers to be exercised by any other body — judiciary remains independent even during President's Rule
Sarkaria Commission and Punchhi Commission recommendations on sparing use of Art. 356 — reform dimension

concepts.name: Financial Emergency (Art. 360): Proclamation and Effects
key_dimensions: Ground: President satisfied that financial stability/credit of India or any part thereof is threatened
Parliamentary approval: both Houses within 2 months by simple majority; once approved, continues indefinitely until revoked (no periodic renewal unlike other emergencies)
Effects: Centre can direct states to observe financial propriety canons; reduce salaries of all government servants including judges of SC and HCs
Trap: Financial Emergency has NEVER been proclaimed in India — and salary reduction of judges is only possible under this, not otherwise

concepts.name: Comparison of Approval Mechanisms Across Three Emergencies
key_dimensions: National Emergency: Special majority (2/3 present+voting AND majority of total membership) in BOTH Houses
President's Rule: Simple majority in both Houses; Rajya Sabha can approve even if Lok Sabha dissolved
Financial Emergency: Simple majority in both Houses within 2 months; no periodic renewal needed after approval
Revocation asymmetry: National Emergency — Lok Sabha alone by simple majority; President's Rule and Financial Emergency — President's discretion, no parliamentary approval needed

concepts.name: 44th Amendment Act (1978): Safeguards Against Emergency Misuse
key_dimensions: 'Internal disturbance' replaced by 'armed rebellion' — raising the threshold for Art. 352
Cabinet's written recommendation made mandatory before Presidential proclamation under Art. 352
Arts. 20 and 21 made non-suspendable even under Art. 359 — right to life and protection against arbitrary conviction are absolute
Art. 19 suspension limited to war/external aggression only, not armed rebellion — 44th Amendment's most tested provision

concepts.name: Suspension of Art. 19 vs. Suspension of Other FRs: Arts. 358 and 359
key_dimensions: Art. 358: Automatic suspension of Art. 19 — no separate order needed; applies only during war or external aggression, NOT armed rebellion
Art. 359: Suspension of other FRs (not Art. 20 and 21) by Presidential order specifying which rights are suspended
Art. 358 suspends Art. 19 for entire duration of emergency; Art. 359 order can specify shorter period
Trap: Under Art. 359, laws made during suspension can be challenged after the order is revoked if they were inconsistent with suspended FRs — ongoing legal validity question

concepts.name: Governor's Role as Trigger vs. Presidential Satisfaction in Art. 356
key_dimensions: Governor's report is ONE basis but not the only basis — President can act 'otherwise' on his own satisfaction
Trap: Governor's report is NOT binding on the President — President may or may not act on it
Misuse pattern: Governors appointed by Centre sending politically motivated reports — Sarkaria Commission critique
Rajasthan case (1977) and subsequent SC rulings on the need for objective material, not just subjective satisfaction

concepts.name: Proclamation During Lok Sabha Dissolution or Recess: Special Rules
key_dimensions: National Emergency can be proclaimed when Lok Sabha is dissolved or in recess — Rajya Sabha alone can approve initially
If only Rajya Sabha approves, Lok Sabha must approve within 30 days of reconstitution, otherwise proclamation ceases
For President's Rule: Rajya Sabha approval is sufficient if Lok Sabha is dissolved — procurement stands for 2 months from reconstitution
Trap: This creates temporary single-House approval — exception to bicameral approval principle that UPSC frequently tests

concepts.name: Scope of Judicial Review of Emergency Proclamations: Evolution
key_dimensions: ADM Jabalpur case (1976): SC held FRs can be completely suspended during emergency — overruled by Justice K.S. Puttaswamy case (2017)
S.R. Bommai (1994): Art. 356 proclamation is justiciable; President's satisfaction must have some rational basis in material before him
National Emergency proclamation: SC can examine whether Cabinet's written advice was given (procedural review) — Minerva Mills precedent
Trap: Revocation of emergency cannot be challenged in court — once revoked, matter is moot; but actions taken during emergency can be challenged

concepts.name: Emergency Provisions and Basic Structure Doctrine
key_dimensions: Kesavananda Bharati (1973): Parliament cannot use emergency to destroy basic structure — limits on Art. 368 apply even during emergency
S.R. Bommai: Secularism and federalism are basic features — Art. 356 cannot be used to undermine these
Emergency provisions themselves cannot be amended to remove judicial review — that would destroy basic structure
Trap: During National Emergency, Parliament can make laws on State List, but cannot permanently transfer subjects from State List to Union List — temporary vs. permanent change
